title: Failure-safe cleanup

sources.locator: SEI CERT C Coding Standard; living standard accessed 2026-07; provisions applicable to Failure-safe cleanup
sources.claim: C resource management assigns clear ownership and routes every success or failure path through cleanup that releases each acquired resource once in reverse dependency order.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Functions that acquire several resources (open a file, allocate a buffer, allocate a result) need **every path**, success or failure, to release exactly what was acquired, in **reverse order**. Early `return`s scattered through the function tend to forget one. The classic C pattern: initialise every resource to a "not acquired" value (`NULL`), and on failure **`goto cleanup`**. The single cleanup section releases each non-NULL resource once, in reverse order, and returns the **first error** that happened. "The OS frees it at exit" isn't an excuse: long-running programs, libraries and loops leak until they fail.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's `process_file` opens a file, allocates a buffer, then returns early on a parse error, leaking both. In a server that processes thousands of files, it eventually runs out of file handles. A function opens a file, allocates a buffer, and on any later failure jumps to one cleanup section that frees the buffer then closes the file. In this lesson you'll repair a multi-resource function to preserve the first failure and release all acquired resources.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Pointers, arrays and arithmetic**, **Structures**, **Allocation and deallocation** and **File streams and binary/text modes**.

sections.heading: The invariant: every acquired resource released once, in reverse
Preserve the first failure

includes: Route every failure through one cleanup section with NULL-initialised resources.
Release in reverse acquisition order and preserve the first error.

examples.title: One exit, every resource released
examples.situation: A function opens a file, allocates a buffer, and on any later failure jumps to one cleanup section that frees the buffer then closes the file.
walkthrough: **A function opens a file, allocates a buffer:** f and buf start NULL and are acquired in order.
**On any later failure jumps to one cleanup section:** a parse error sets status and does goto cleanup.
**That frees the buffer then closes the file:** reverse order; with -fsanitize=address, no leak will be reported on any path.
examples.result: Thousands of files are processed without running out of handles or memory.

examples.title: The overwritten error
examples.situation: A cleanup section sets status = fclose(f) unconditionally, so every parse error is reported as "success" because fclose returned 0.
walkthrough: The later, successful fclose erased the real failure.
Only update status from cleanup if status is still OK.
Test each failure path and check the returned code.
examples.result: Callers see the error that actually happened.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The operating system eventually reclaims resources, so cleanup on error paths is unnecessary in a C program.
misconceptions.correction: Programs that keep running, loop, or are used as libraries leak on each failure until they exhaust memory or handles. Every path must release what it acquired.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, what did the server eventually run out of?

analogy.example: Cleanup is like **leaving a campsite**. Whatever happens (great trip or a storm cut it short), you pack up everything you set up, in reverse: take down the tarp before the poles it hangs from. And the trip report says what went wrong first, not "the car was a bit muddy".
usefulFor: remembering pack up on every exit
limitations: Campsites have rangers; C has only sanitizers.
Items you never unpacked (NULL) need no packing.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing failure-safe cleanup. Step 1, Acquire: f is open; buf is allocated. The function opens a file and allocates a buffer, in order. Step 2, Fail: status is ERR_READ. On any later failure it jumps to one cleanup section. Step 3, Release: buf is freed; f is closed; returned is ERR_READ. Cleanup frees the buffer then closes the file, keeping the first error.

nearTransfer.prompt: Refactor a function with three early returns that leak into the NULL-init + goto cleanup pattern. Force each failure (missing file, malloc wrapper returning NULL, bad content) and confirm no leaks with -fsanitize=address.
scaffold: Check the returned status each time.

farTransfer.prompt: Write copy_file(src, dst) that opens two files and allocates a buffer, copies in chunks, handles every read, write and close failure, removes a partial dst on failure, and returns the first error. Test every failure path.
expectedEvidence: No partial output left on failure.

remediation.explanation: For a multi-resource function list: **each resource, where it's acquired, and where it's released on every path.** If any path lacks a release, route it through cleanup.

recap.summary: To repair a multi-resource function, initialise every resource to a not-acquired value, send every failure to one cleanup section, release each acquired resource once in reverse order, and preserve the first error instead of letting later cleanup results overwrite it.
